title: An opening is a route to a structure and its plans
outcomes: Explains that different move orders can reach one pawn structure, and that the structure suggests plans
Chooses a plan-consistent move for the Carlsbad, isolated-pawn and open-centre structures
Sees that the same pawn push can work in one structure and fail in another

steps.text: An opening is a route to a **structure**: the shape of the pawns. Pawns cannot go back, so the shape changes only slowly, by pushes and captures, and it says where pieces belong and which pawn pushes matter. Different move orders can reach the same structure. Learn a few structures and their usual plans, and many openings become one problem.

steps.caption: Route A. White's c-pawn is gone from the board and Black has no e-pawn.
Route B starts with a different first move but ends in exactly the same position.

steps.text: **Carlsbad:** White has no c-pawn, and Black has a pawn on d5 and usually one on c6 (it may still stand on c7). White often pushes the queenside pawns (b4, then b5) to create a target on c6, or trades pieces. Black often repositions a knight toward the kingside or trades pieces. These are usual plans, not laws.

**Isolated d-pawn:** a pawn on d4 with no friendly pawn on the c or e file. Pawns cannot defend it, but it gives space and open lines. The owner usually keeps pieces on and aims them at the king. The other side adds pressure, blockades d5 and trades pieces. Tendencies, not laws.

steps.title: The same push in different structures
steps.prompt: A plan belongs to a structure. Predict where a queenside pawn push fits, then check.

steps.text: **Open centre:** the central pawns are traded and files and diagonals are open. Speed and king safety count most. Put rooks on open files and develop before you attack. These are tendencies; check what the opponent's last move attacks first.

steps.prompt: Pick an opening you play. Which structure does it usually lead to, and what is the usual plan for each side? Write one sentence for each.
